meaning: A declaration of unshakeable dominance — a challenge to anyone who fancies standing in the Bariga upstart's way.
context: The 2010 breakout that launched him. Patience and grind delivered entirely in Yoruba, when that was still a commercial risk — and the blueprint every street-hop record after it borrowed from.

meaning: Olamide's own tag and the crowd's call-back — an alias that became a greeting the streets used on his behalf.
context: Carried by the Baddest Guy Ever Liveth run, when the centre of gravity in Nigerian hip-hop moved from Victoria Island boardrooms to the Mainland.

meaning: The Mainland dance wave that became 2014's default party instruction — arms low, knees bent, everybody at once.
context: Carried nationally by the Lil Kesh remix Olamide guested on, months after YBNL unveiled Kesh and Viktoh. Proof the label could turn a Mainland step into a countrywide reflex.

literal: Shake-it, bobo — a called-out dance stance
meaning: The arm-crossover leg step that ran Lagos parties through 2015, named by the hook that instructed it.
context: Off Eyan Mayweather, closing a year of running the street unopposed. The move outlived the record — a reception-floor staple long after the single cycled out.

literal: Child of the hood / street disciple
meaning: An identity badge for Mainland youth — claiming the street as a lineage rather than an address.
context: A roll call more than a single. By the Street King run it worked as a greeting: one word that told you where somebody stood.

meaning: A single-syllable command that doubled as a dance cue — the shaku shaku era's starting pistol.
context: Shot in Bariga with local dancers and built into the #WoChallenge, it was large enough that Wizkid called it the biggest Nigerian song of the year. Shaku shaku left Agege and entered the national bloodstream.

meaning: Street shorthand for someone mixing their own intoxicants — chemistry repurposed as a label for a nightlife habit.
context: A 2018 non-album single, released in the year he stepped back from albums and let loose singles carry the argument. Its subject drew enough scrutiny that Olamide had to state publicly it was a caution, not an endorsement.
